rationale: The lament's preface names Israel's captivity and Jerusalem's devastation; Kings narrates the burning of Jerusalem and removal of its remaining people. This supplies the historical catastrophe over which the city is personified as bereaved.

Jerusalem's friends act faithlessly and leave her without comfort; Jeremiah describes the afflicted people forgotten by all their friends, who will not inquire after them. Both portray stricken people abandoned by those expected to help.

Judea lives among nations without finding rest; Deuteronomy warns of scattering among nations with no rest or resting place for the foot. The lament repeats the exile-and-restlessness pattern of the warning.

relationship: Festival life brought to an end
rationale: Zion's roads mourn because nobody comes for the festival; the next lament says the Lord destroyed His festival and forgot festival and Sabbath in Zion. Both describe the loss of the city's gathered worship.
The lament connects Judah's ungodliness with her infants going into captivity; Deuteronomy warns that sons and daughters will go into captivity rather than remain with their parents.

Zion's rulers go weakly before the pursuer; Kings describes the fleeing king overtaken by the Chaldean army, with his force scattering away from him. The narrative supplies a concrete parallel to the lament's defeated leadership.

Jerusalem's enemies laugh at her deportation; the psalm of the ravaged city describes its people becoming the neighbors' sneering and ridicule. Both add humiliation by onlookers to the city's material losses.

The lament links Jerusalem's sin with former admirers seeing her shame; Ezekiel portrays Jerusalem's lawlessness being exposed before her lovers, who strip her and leave her exposed. The passages share the city's personified humiliation.
Both verses say the comforter is absent while the enemy has grown strong. The repeated combination links the city's plea to be seen with her later explanation of her tears.
The lament sees foreign nations entering the sanctuary and taking desired things; the psalm likewise says nations entered God's inheritance and defiled His holy temple in Jerusalem.

The people seek bread and exchange desired possessions for food; Kings records famine so severe in besieged Jerusalem that no loaves remained for the people. The narrative explains the crisis behind the lament's desperate search for food.

The suffering city asks road-passers to turn and see her pain; later those passing along the road clap, hiss and shake their heads at Jerusalem. The repeated audience responds with mockery rather than the requested recognition of suffering.

relationship: Divine judgment as a capturing net
rationale: The Lord spreads a net for the lamenting city's feet; Ezekiel says He will spread His net over the ruler and bring him to Babylon. Both represent judgment and capture through a divine net, at different personal scales.

relationship: Sin as an overwhelming bodily burden
rationale: The lament's acts of ungodliness rise upon the neck as strength fails; the psalm describes lawless deeds rising above the head and weighing like a heavy load. The connection preserves the lament's wording without inserting an unmentioned yoke.

The Lord treads a winepress for Daughter Judah; Isaiah depicts wrathful trampling through the image of clothes from a trodden winepress. The violent judgment image is shared while the identified recipients differ.

The lamenting city's tears accompany destroyed sons and an absent comforter; Jeremiah portrays Rachel weeping over sons who are no more, followed by a promise of return from enemy territory. Both connect parental lament with the loss of children.

Zion stretches out her hands without finding comfort; the later appeal urges lifted hands before the Lord for the lives of starving infants. Both place outstretched or lifted hands within the distressed city's appeal for help.

The lament confesses that the Lord is righteous while the speaker admits embittering His mouth; Nehemiah's communal prayer likewise confesses God's righteousness in the calamities and the people's grievous sin.
The city calls her lovers but is deceived; Jeremiah says the afflicted people's friends forgot them and will not inquire. Both deny the hoped-for aid from former companions while the city suffers.

The lament contrasts bereavement by the sword outside with death inside the house; Ezekiel explicitly places the sword outside and famine and death inside the city. The paired inside-outside threats closely correspond.

The enemies rejoice over the city's calamity but are described as becoming like her; Jeremiah declares that devourers will be devoured and plunderers become plunder. Both portray oppressors receiving the treatment they inflicted.

relationship: Groaning joined to a plea for repayment
rationale: The lament asks that the enemies' wickedness come before God and be repaid amid many groans; the psalm asks God to hear captives' groaning and repay the neighbors' insults. Both join distress to a petition for retribution.

relationship: Sanctuary as the place of God's feet
rationale: The Lord does not remember His footstool in Zion's catastrophe; David describes the planned ark-house as a standing place for the Lord's feet. This supports the sanctuary imagery in the lament without describing a literal divine body.

relationship: Destruction of the royal and fortified city
rationale: The lament portrays Judah's strongholds cast down and her king and rulers profaned; Jeremiah records the burning of the royal house and demolition of Jerusalem's wall. The narrative supplies concrete counterparts to the collapse of the fortified royal city.

relationship: Repeated divine fire against the city
rationale: The Lord's anger kindles consuming fire in Jacob; the later lament says His furious anger kindled fire in Zion that consumed her foundations. Both descriptions make the city's burning an expression of divine fury.

The Lord draws His bow like an enemy and makes His right hand firm like an opponent; Isaiah says the people's disobedience caused Him to turn hostile and fight them. Both portray divine opposition toward His own people.

relationship: The Lord fighting against the city
rationale: The lament calls the Lord an enemy who destroys Israel's citadels; Jeremiah records His declaration that He Himself will fight the people with mighty arm, fury and indignation. Both attribute the catastrophe to divine opposition.

The lament says festival and Sabbath are forgotten in Zion under God's anger; Hosea announces the removal of rejoicing, festivals, new moons, Sabbaths and assemblies. Both make the loss of festal worship part of judgment.

relationship: Enemies profaning the sanctuary and feast
rationale: Enemies raise a shout in the rejected sanctuary as on a festival day; the psalm describes enemies boasting within God's feast, tearing down the sanctuary and burning it. Both invert the sacred celebration through hostile intrusion.

relationship: A measure used for Jerusalem's judgment
rationale: The Lord stretches out a measure while destroying Zion's wall; Kings announces that He will stretch Samaria's measure over Jerusalem. Both use measurement as an image of deliberate judgment upon the city.

The lament says the prophets saw no vision from the Lord; the sanctuary lament in Psalms says no signs were seen and there is no prophet any longer. Both include absent prophetic guidance among the community's losses.

relationship: Silent mourning with dust and torn or mourning clothes
rationale: Zion's elders sit silently with dust on their heads and sackcloth; Job's friends weep, tear their robes, sprinkle earth on themselves and sit without speaking. The gestures of bodily abasement and silence express overwhelming grief in both scenes.

relationship: Tears over the shattered daughter of the people
rationale: The speaker's tears and inward distress arise from the shattering of the daughter of his people; Jeremiah likewise joins that daughter's crushing with inward pain and a wish for eyes flowing with tears.

Children ask their mothers for grain and wine as they weaken; the later lament depicts nursing children thirsty and infants asking for bread with nobody to break it. Both focus the famine through children's unmet requests.

relationship: Rhetorical question about healing the people
rationale: The lament asks who can heal Jerusalem's great crushing; Jeremiah asks whether there is resin or a physician and why the daughter of the people is not healed. Both express the community's apparently unrelieved injury through a healing question.

relationship: False prophecy failing to turn people from evil
rationale: The prophets' futile visions failed to uncover injustice and avert captivity; Jeremiah condemns invented visions and says true hearing would have turned the people from evil practices. Both connect false prophecy with failure to confront wrongdoing.

Passersby mock Jerusalem by asking whether this is the city they will call the gladness of all the earth. The psalm praises God's city and Zion as exultation for all the earth; that celebratory description becomes a taunt in the lament.

relationship: Enemies opening their mouths and claiming to swallow
rationale: Jerusalem's enemies open their mouths and boast that they swallowed her. The psalm reports enemies opening their mouths and exulting at what they see, then prays that they not boast of swallowing the sufferer. The actual and feared taunts closely correspond.

The lament says the Lord carried out His intention and fulfilled His ancient words; Jeremiah describes the city handed to Chaldeans through sword and famine and says that what God spoke happened. Both interpret the catastrophe as fulfillment of His warning.

Zion is urged to let tears flow day and night without pause; Jeremiah wishes for a head of water and fountain-like eyes to weep day and night for the wounded people. The unceasing-tears imagery closely corresponds.

relationship: Pouring out the heart before God
rationale: The lament urges the people to pour out the heart like water before the Lord; the psalm tells the whole assembly to pour out their hearts before Him. Both describe open communal prayer through the same pouring metaphor.

relationship: The horror of children becoming food
rationale: The lament asks whether women will eat the fruit of their womb; the later lament states that compassionate women's hands boiled their children for food during the people's shattering. The later statement provides the explicit counterpart to the question.

relationship: Young and old caught in Jerusalem's fall
rationale: The lament describes child and elder lying at the way out and young people taken captive; Chronicles describes young men killed, virgins shown no mercy and elders carried away. Both portray the catastrophe across age groups while preserving different details.

A festival day is called, but on the Lord's day of anger nobody is rescued; the earlier lament says He called a time against Judah to crush its chosen men. Both turn the language of a summoned occasion toward the city's calamity.
